title: A Question You Must Answer Before The First Day Of School
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that teachers often enter the school year with only a vague sense of what they want students to be doing moment to moment, and that this fogginess directly produces sloppy, unclear expectations and correspondingly poor student performance. His proposed solution, borrowed from fields like professional sports, medicine, and elite cooking, is visualization: deliberately closing one's eyes and mentally rehearsing, in specific detail, exactly what a successful lesson, transition, or activity should look like before teaching it. He is careful to distinguish this from wishful thinking, noting that visualization should only cover what is within the teacher's control, not hoped-for miracles. Practically, he recommends visualizing each block of the day — how students enter, sit, listen, work in groups, ask questions — and then teaching, modeling, and explaining that vision until it materializes in the classroom, arguing that any deviation from a clearly visualized standard becomes immediately noticeable and correctable.
points: Vague, foggy expectations about what students should be doing moment-to-moment directly produce sloppy, unclear performance from them.
Visualization — closing one's eyes to mentally rehearse a lesson, transition, or activity in specific detail — is proposed as the practical fix.
Visualization should cover only what is within the teacher's control, not wished-for outcomes or miracles.
The technique is compared to practices used by elite professionals like athletes, doctors, and chefs, and cited as nearly as effective as actual practice.
Deliberately visualizing before teaching an expectation makes any later deviation from that standard immediately noticeable and correctable.
quotes: Question: How do you know what you want your students to do from one moment to the next?
Tom Brady knows what every player’s role is right down to their foot and hand placement.
Okay, before you roll your eyes and assume we’re talking about the law of attraction or some other new-agey trend, know that visualization has been shown to be nearly as effective as actual practice.
All it entails is closing your eyes and rehearsing what you want to happen. The exercise, however, doesn’t involve hope. You’re not visualizing miracles or improbabilities.
Visualization is so powerful, in fact, especially when it becomes a habit, that anything you visualize will appear almost as it did in your mind’s eye.
